tasks.description: Write a few lines to 'notes.txt' first (using open with 'w'), then read the whole file back and print its contents.
tasks.hint:
Write: `with open('notes.txt', 'w') as f: f.write('Hello\nWorld')`
Read: `with open('notes.txt', 'r') as f: print(f.read())`
The `with` statement automatically closes the file — always use it.
tasks.solution:
with open('notes.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Hello\n')
    f.write('World\n')

with open('notes.txt', 'r') as f:
    print(f.read())
tasks.walkthrough:
The first `with` block opens the file for writing and puts two lines in it. The block ending closes the file.
The second opens it for reading and `read()` returns the whole contents as one string.

tasks.description: Write 5 lines to 'numbers.txt' (each containing a number 1-5), then read each line and print it stripped of whitespace.
tasks.hint:
Write with a loop: `for i in range(1, 6): f.write(f'{i}\n')`
Read: `for line in f: print(line.strip())` — the `.strip()` removes the trailing newline.
Without strip, each `print()` adds its own newline, causing blank lines.
tasks.walkthrough:
The loop writes 1 to 5, each followed by a newline.
Reading back, each `line` still includes that newline, so `.strip()` removes it before printing.

tasks.description: Write a poem of 4+ lines to 'poem.txt'. Read it back and print each line with its line number: '1: First line'
tasks.hint:
`enumerate(iterable, start=1)` gives you (number, item) pairs starting at 1.
`for i, line in enumerate(f, 1): print(f'{i}: {line.strip()}')`
The second arg to enumerate sets the starting number.
tasks.solution:
with open('poem.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('The fog comes\n')
    f.write('on little cat feet.\n')
    f.write('It sits looking\n')
    f.write('over harbor and city\n')

with open('poem.txt', 'r') as f:
    for number, line in enumerate(f, 1):
        print(f'{number}: {line.strip()}')
tasks.walkthrough:
`enumerate(f, 1)` pairs each line with a number starting from 1 rather than 0.
The two values are unpacked into `number` and `line` on each pass.

tasks.description: Write a sentence to 'words.txt'. Read it back and count how many words it contains. Print the word count.
tasks.hint:
Read the whole file: `content = f.read()`
`.split()` splits on any whitespace and returns a list of words.
`len(content.split())` counts the words.
tasks.solution:
with open('words.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog')

with open('words.txt', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()
    print(len(content.split()))
tasks.walkthrough:
`.split()` with no argument breaks the text at any whitespace, giving a list of words.
`len()` counts them: 9.

tasks.description: Append a new line to an existing file using mode 'a'. Then read the whole file and print it.
tasks.hint:
Mode `'a'` (append) adds to the END of a file without deleting existing content.
Include `\n` at the start of your new text: `f.write('\nNew line here')`
Then open with `'r'` and `f.read()` to see the full file.
tasks.solution:
with open('journal.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Day one')

with open('journal.txt', 'a') as f:
    f.write('\nDay two')

with open('journal.txt', 'r') as f:
    print(f.read())
tasks.walkthrough:
The middle block opens in append mode, so the existing text is kept and the new text goes after it.
The leading `\n` starts the new entry on its own line.

tasks.description: Write 5 names to 'names.txt' (one per line). Read them back and print only names longer than 4 characters.
tasks.hint:
Read with `f.readlines()` → list of lines, each ending with `\n`.
Strip each: `name = line.strip()`
Filter: `if len(name) > 4: print(name)`
tasks.walkthrough:
`readlines()` returns all the lines as a list. Each is stripped to remove the newline before its length is measured.
Only names longer than four characters pass the check.

lesson.intro:
Programs that only live in memory forget everything when they end. Files let
them remember. Today you'll write a little text to a file and read it back in
a few different ways.

In this app, files you create end up in the `src/workspace` folder, and they
stay there between runs, so you can write in one run and read in the next.

sections.heading: open, with, and the mode
sections.body:
`open(name, mode)` opens a file. The mode is `'w'` to write (which wipes any
existing content), `'r'` to read, or `'a'` to append. Wrapping it in `with`
means the file is closed automatically at the end of the block, even if
something goes wrong. Always use `with`.
sections.code:
with open('notes.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('First line\n')
    f.write('Second line\n')

with open('notes.txt', 'r') as f:
    print(f.read())

sections.heading: Reading line by line
sections.body:
Looping over an open file gives you one line at a time. Each line still ends
with its newline character, so `.strip()` it before printing, or you'll get
blank lines between them.

sections.heading: Numbering lines with enumerate
sections.body: `enumerate(f, 1)` pairs each line with a counter starting at 1.
sections.code:
with open('poem.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Roses are red\nViolets are blue\n')

with open('poem.txt') as f:
    for i, line in enumerate(f, 1):
        print(f'{i}: {line.strip()}')
sections.output:
1: Roses are red
2: Violets are blue

sections.heading: Appending
sections.body:
Mode `'a'` adds to the end of a file without touching what's already there.
If the existing content doesn't end with a newline, start your new text with
one.
sections.code:
with open('log.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('start')

with open('log.txt', 'a') as f:
    f.write('\nmore')

with open('log.txt') as f:
    print(f.read())

watch_out: `'w'` mode empties the file the moment you open it. Use `'a'` if you want to keep what's there.
`f.write()` doesn't add a newline. Put `\n` in the string yourself.
Reading after the `with` block ends gives 'I/O operation on closed file'. Keep the reads inside.
`f.read()` can only be called once per open; the second call returns an empty string.
